description: How participation in sport supports physical health, mental health and social wellbeing.
content_html:
What Do We Mean by Health and Wellbeing?

Health is not simply the absence of illness. The World Health Organisation defines it as a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing — a definition that has shaped how GCSE PE approaches this topic. A person can be physically fit (able to run five kilometres without stopping) yet struggle with anxiety, loneliness or low self-worth. True wellbeing is multi-dimensional, and physical activity affects all three dimensions simultaneously, which is what makes it one of the most powerful public health tools available.

This lesson examines each dimension in turn: physical health, mental health and social health. Each is an equal component of overall wellbeing, and a physically active lifestyle improves all three.

Key Fact

Participation in physical activity improves health across three dimensions: physical (heart function, body systems, disease prevention), mental (stress reduction, hormone release, emotional control) and social (friendships, teamwork, community). These three dimensions are interconnected — improving one often improves the others.

Physical Health and Wellbeing

The physical benefits of regular exercise are the most visible and the most extensively researched. Regular aerobic activity — whether swimming, cycling, running or team sport — strengthens the heart muscle, increases stroke volume (the amount of blood ejected with each heartbeat) and reduces resting heart rate. The result is a more efficient cardiovascular system that can deliver oxygen to working muscles more effectively during exercise and recover more quickly afterwards. Athletes who train consistently over years develop bradycardia, a resting heart rate well below the population average of 70 beats per minute.

Beyond the heart, regular exercise improves the efficiency of the respiratory system, the musculoskeletal system and the immune system. The lungs become more efficient at gas exchange; muscles grow stronger and more fatigue-resistant; bones maintain their density and reduce the risk of osteoporosis in later life. These systemic benefits mean a physically active person is better equipped to perform everyday tasks (carrying shopping, climbing stairs, walking to work) and is less likely to suffer from a range of chronic diseases including type 2 diabetes, certain cancers and hypertension.

One of the clearest population-level physical benefits of exercise is its role in weight management. Regular activity burns calories, maintains muscle mass and supports a healthy body composition. This helps avoid obesity, which is itself a risk factor for heart disease, diabetes and reduced mobility. The physical and the social are already beginning to connect: an individual who maintains a healthy weight through sport is also likely to have the physical capacity to engage with others in activity, creating a positive feedback loop.

Mental Health and Wellbeing

The mental health benefits of exercise are now backed by a substantial body of clinical research and are increasingly recognised by healthcare systems as a legitimate treatment for mild-to-moderate anxiety and depression. The mechanisms are both biochemical and psychological.

At the biochemical level, moderate to vigorous exercise triggers the release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of happiness and calm. It also promotes the release of endorphins — natural pain-relieving chemicals that produce the so-called “runner’s high” familiar to distance athletes. The neurological effect of these hormones is a measurable reduction in perceived stress and anxiety. For many individuals, a vigorous training session or team sport match functions as a reliable, accessible and side-effect-free stress management tool.

Beyond hormones, physical activity provides psychological benefits through mastery and control. Setting a personal best, learning a new skill or winning a team competition builds self-efficacy — the belief in one’s own capacity to succeed. This is particularly powerful for young people, for whom sporting achievement can become a foundation for confidence in other areas of life. The ability to control emotions during competition (remain calm under pressure, manage frustration after a mistake) transfers directly to emotional regulation in daily life. These mental benefits are why sport is used therapeutically in programmes for young people experiencing mental health difficulties.

Stress is the body’s physiological response to a perceived threat or challenge. When stressed, the hypothalamus activates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones raise heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, preparing the body for action. In short bursts this is useful; chronically elevated stress hormones damage the cardiovascular system, suppress immunity and impair sleep.

Exercise provides the body with a “legitimate outlet” for the physiological state stress creates. A run or a football training session allows the body to use the elevated heart rate and glucose productively. After exercise, serotonin and endorphin levels remain elevated for hours, creating a period of improved mood and reduced anxiety. Over time, regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol levels and a faster physiological return to calm after stressful events. This is why mental health professionals increasingly recommend structured physical activity as a first-line intervention for mild anxiety.

Social Health and Wellbeing

Humans are social animals. The sense of belonging to a group, having friends and being valued by a community are fundamental psychological needs. Sport and physical activity are remarkably powerful vehicles for meeting these needs, which is why social health is a genuine and distinct category in the wellbeing framework.

Team sports in particular demand cooperation and teamwork. Playing in a netball team, a cricket XI or a rowing eight requires communication, trust, shared responsibility and collective problem-solving. These are not merely sporting skills: they are life skills transferable to workplaces, families and communities. Young people who participate in team sport regularly develop stronger interpersonal skills and a better understanding of how to negotiate conflict constructively.

Participation also creates opportunities to socialise and make friends. For individuals who are isolated — whether through geography, disability, mental health difficulties or life transitions such as moving to a new school — joining a sports club can be the single most effective intervention for reducing loneliness. Sport provides a structured social context with shared purpose, which lowers the social anxiety of unstructured socialisation. Community sport clubs also play a direct role in meeting basic social needs by connecting individuals to wider networks of mutual support.

Students sometimes assume that wellbeing benefits require competitive, high-intensity sport. This is not what the spec says, and it is not supported by the evidence. The physical, mental and social benefits of physical activity are available across a spectrum from gentle recreational walking through to elite competition. What matters is regular participation, not intensity or competitive context.

Indeed, for some individuals — particularly those recovering from mental health difficulties, or older adults entering exercise for the first time — low-intensity, non-competitive activity (yoga, social swimming, walking groups) may produce greater wellbeing gains precisely because it is accessible, enjoyable and sustainable. The spec asks you to recognise that physical activity broadly encompasses all forms of movement, not just sport.

Key Fact

For extended-response questions on wellbeing, make sure you address all three dimensions with a sporting example for each. A common error is to write only about physical benefits. Mental (serotonin, stress, emotional control) and social (teamwork, cooperation, socialisation) benefits carry equal mark-scheme weight.
exam_tip_html: For 6-mark analyse questions on wellbeing, the most frequent error is covering physical benefits thoroughly while barely mentioning mental or social health. Examiners design mark schemes with points spread across all three dimensions. Structure your answer in three clear sections: physical, mental, social. For each, identify a benefit, explain the mechanism (e.g. serotonin for mental; cooperation for social), and anchor it to a sporting example. For 3-mark describe questions (e.g. “Describe how participation in sport improves mental health”), use three distinct points: one for the hormonal/biochemical mechanism, one for psychological benefit (confidence, emotional control), one for the sporting context. Avoid writing the same point twice with slightly different wording — the mark scheme will not credit near-identical answers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Physical participation improves cardiovascular efficiency, reduces disease risk and supports healthy weight management — all improving physical health and wellbeing.
  • Exercise releases serotonin and endorphins, reduces cortisol levels and builds self-efficacy, delivering substantial and evidence-based mental health benefits.
  • Team sport and group activity foster cooperation, teamwork and socialisation, directly addressing social health needs and reducing loneliness.

practice_questions.text: Identify one mental health benefit of regular participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: reduces stress or tension; release of serotonin/endorphins (feel-good hormones); helps control emotions; reduces anxiety; improves mood. Accept precise physiological answers (serotonin release) or descriptive answers (reduces stress).

1 mark for a basic definition: the ability to form relationships with others / meet social needs. 1 mark for development: includes the ability to cooperate with others, belong to a community and contribute to group goals; or gives a sporting example (e.g. playing in a team sport provides social contact and a sense of belonging).

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways in which participating in team sport can improve a young person's social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for three distinct points from: provides opportunities to socialise and make friends; develops cooperation skills (working with others towards a shared goal); develops teamwork (collective effort, shared responsibility); reduces loneliness / combats isolation; connects individuals to a community network; helps develop communication and trust.

practice_questions.text: Explain how regular exercise can improve a person's mental health, referring to at least one biological mechanism.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a benefit (reduces stress / anxiety / improves mood). 1 mark for the biological mechanism (exercise triggers release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of calm and happiness). 1 mark for a second mechanism or further development (endorphins also released, producing feelings of euphoria; or regular exercise lowers baseline cortisol levels over time). 1 mark for sporting application (a swimmer who trains regularly may find their anxiety levels reduced on school days as a result of consistent serotonin release).

practice_questions.text: A table shows the self-reported wellbeing scores (out of 10) of 40 students before and after a 6-week exercise programme: Physical wellbeing — before 5.2, after 7.1; Mental wellbeing — before 4.8, after 6.9; Social wellbeing — before 5.5, after 7.4. Using the data, calculate the mean improvement across all three dimensions of wellbeing, and explain what this suggests about the value of the programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: improvements are 1.9 (physical), 2.1 (mental), 1.9 (social); mean = (1.9 + 2.1 + 1.9) ÷ 3 = 5.9 ÷ 3 = 1.97 (accept 1.96 to 2.0). 1 mark for showing working and stating the unit (points on the wellbeing scale). 1 mark for a valid inference: the mean improvement of approximately 2 points across all three wellbeing dimensions suggests the programme produced balanced benefits, indicating that physical activity supports physical, mental and social health simultaneously.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how participation in physical activity can improve physical, mental and social wellbeing. Refer to specific mechanisms in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): analyses all three wellbeing dimensions with at least one specific mechanism per dimension; applies each point to a sporting example; links mechanisms to outcomes (e.g. exercise raises serotonin, which reduces anxiety, which improves daily functioning); reaches a developed analytical conclusion about the interconnected nature of the three dimensions.
Secure (3–4 marks): covers at least two dimensions with some development; sporting context mostly present; mechanisms mentioned but not fully explained.
Developing (2 marks): identifies benefits across two or more dimensions but mainly descriptive; limited sporting application.
Emerging (1 mark): one dimension only or very basic points with no sporting context.

knowledge_checks.q: Which neurotransmitter released during exercise is linked to feelings of happiness and reduced stress?
Which term describes a lower-than-average resting heart rate caused by long-term aerobic training?
Working jointly with others towards a shared goal, adjusting individual behaviour to serve the team, is called _____.
Regular physical activity helps meet _____ health needs by providing opportunities to make friends and belong to a community.
Match each wellbeing dimension to the correct benefit of physical activity:
right: Improves heart function and reduces risk of chronic disease
Releases serotonin and helps control emotions
Develops cooperation, teamwork and opportunities to make friends

flashcard_questions.a: The condition of the body and its ability to function effectively, free from illness or injury.
The condition of the mind and emotions, including managing stress and maintaining a positive outlook.
The ability to form positive relationships, contribute to a community and meet social needs.

flashcard_questions.q: What is serotonin and why is it important in exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: A brain neurotransmitter released during exercise that promotes feelings of happiness and calm.
A lower resting heart rate from long-term aerobic training — the heart pumps more blood per beat.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two physical health benefits of regular exercise.
flashcard_questions.a: Stronger heart muscle, reduced risk of diabetes, lower blood pressure, improved immune function.
Exercise releases serotonin and endorphins, lowering cortisol and improving mood for hours after activity.
Working jointly with others towards a shared goal, adjusting individual behaviour to serve the team.
Combined effort of a group where collective performance exceeds what individuals achieve alone.

flashcard_questions.q: How does team sport reduce loneliness?
flashcard_questions.a: It provides a structured social context with shared purpose, lowering barriers to forming friendships.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two emotional/psychological benefits of exercise.
flashcard_questions.a: Improved self-efficacy (confidence), better emotional control, reduced anxiety, improved mood.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are all three wellbeing dimensions important to cover in an exam answer?
flashcard_questions.a: Mark schemes award equal weight to physical, mental and social benefits — ignoring one loses marks.

glossary_terms.definition: The condition of the body and its ability to function effectively, free from illness or injury.
The condition of the mind and emotions, including the ability to manage stress, maintain a positive outlook and function in daily life.
The ability to form and maintain positive relationships with others, contribute to a community and meet social needs.
A neurotransmitter produced in the brain during exercise that contributes to feelings of happiness, calm and wellbeing.
A lower-than-average resting heart rate caused by long-term aerobic training, as the heart becomes more efficient and pumps more blood per beat.
Working jointly with others towards a shared goal, adjusting individual behaviour to serve the team.
The combined effort of a group working together, where the collective outcome exceeds what individuals could achieve alone.
